newsitem.title: CANADA: Ballard says talks to other automakers.
newsitem.headline: Ballard says talks to other automakers.

text.p: Canada's Ballard Power Systems Inc, which recently sold a 25 percent stake to Daimler-Benz AG, said Thursday that it was talking to other automakers about the possibility of striking another similar deal.

"We have had some discussions with other auto companies and some (discussions) are still continuing to see the possibility of bringing in another partner," Ballard President Firoz Rasul told the company's annual meeting.

He told Reuters after the meeting that the discussions were continuing with companies who already have contracts with Ballard, which is developing "fuel cell" technology that converts fuel into electricity with little pollution.

The list of automakers who have development contracts with Ballard include General Motors Corp, Chrysler Corp, Ford Motor Co, Honda Motor Co Ltd and Nissan Motor Co Ltd and Ballard said it counts eight of the world's top 16 automakers as its customers.
Rasul declined to specify which of the companies are involved in talks about expanding their relationship with Ballard.

But he said Ballard's deal with Daimler would not allow the German company to block entrance of another car maker. Instead, Ballard has emphasized to Daimler the potential positives of enlisting another partner.
"By having perhaps another auto company involved, it would be advantageous," Rasul said.

Ballard and Daimler-Benz announced a US$333 million deal in April aimed at bringing a new electric car to market in eight years. Under the agreement, Daimler takes a 25-percent stake in Ballard and the two companies will seek to commercialize fuel-cell technology.

Fuel cells, which run on fuel such as hydrogen and methanol, are already powering prototype buses and cars. Daimler and Ballard plan to market the technology to other car companies around the world, although Daimler's Mercedes division is expected to launch its own car based on the engine system.

Ballard's deal with Daimler gives the German company the right to maintain its ownership in Ballard at 25 percent and not be diluted by future deals. Rasul said Ballard does not believe Daimler is interested in a full takeover of Ballard because that could jeopardize Ballard's entrepreneurial culture.
"They feel they will get a much greater return by continuing to be a partner rather than an owner," he said.
While the company said it sees no sign of any looming takeover interest, shareholders at the meeting approved a shareholder rights plan.

Rasul told shareholders that the company's main drive is to reduce the cost of fuel cell engines to one-tenth their present level so they can be widely commercialized. Daimler is targeting initial production of 100,000 units.
"To reduce the cost, that is the real challenge," Rasul said. Once cost goals are reached "then the world is our oyster."
Competition to bring fuel cells to market is intensifying but analysts believe Ballard has about a three-year lead over its rivals. "We will be first in the marketplace," Rasul said.

Automotive analysts have said the two companies face an uphill struggle to gain consumer acceptance for their electric car and believe it will take longer than eight years to build demand for the vehicles, although stringent air-quality regulations could speed their spread.
Ballard is also seeking to find partners this year to develop fuel cells for stationary power generation such as at factories, and for portable, marine, space and other applications in the future.
The company's plan calls for it to report its first profit between 2000 and 2002.
